# Method for Manufacturing Press Components from Ultra-High Tensile Strength Steel Sheet

## Overview

This method enables the manufacture of a press component from an ultra-high tensile strength steel sheet without generating cracks in the flange located on the inner circumferential side of the curved portion. Forming components with curved geometries from ultra-high tensile strength steel presents significant challenges, particularly in the flange regions where material behavior is most critical. This approach addresses those challenges through a carefully controlled forming process.

## The Forming Process

The manufacturing process employs cold press working combined with a free bending method applied to the steel sheet blank. By using cold press working, the method maintains the inherent strength properties of the ultra-high tensile strength steel, while the free bending technique provides the flexibility needed to accommodate the demanding deformation requirements of the curved geometry.

## Material Inflow Facilitating Portion

A key feature of this method is the creation of a material inflow facilitating portion during press working. This dedicated portion is specifically designed to improve material flow into the critical flange area, where cracking is most likely to occur during conventional forming operations.

The facilitating portion functions by increasing the amount by which the blank's end portion flows into the region that forms the inner circumferential flange of the curved section. By promoting this additional material inflow, the method ensures that sufficient material is available in the flange area, thereby reducing the localized strain that would otherwise lead to crack formation.

## Strategic Positioning

To achieve its intended effect, the material inflow facilitating portion is positioned near the blank area that becomes the flange on the inner circumferential side of the curved portion. This strategic placement ensures that the enhanced material flow is directed precisely to the location where it is most needed, allowing the process to reliably produce crack-free components even when working with ultra-high tensile strength steel.

# Manufacturing Press Components from Ultra-High Tensile Strength Steel Sheets

## Background and Technical Challenge

The manufacturing of press components from ultra-high tensile strength steel sheets presents significant technical challenges, particularly when forming parts with curved geometries. During the forming process, cracks frequently develop in the flange region located on the inner circumferential side of curved portions. These defects arise because the material in this area is subjected to compressive stresses that exceed the deformation capacity of ultra-high tensile strength steel, which, while offering excellent strength characteristics, tends to have limited formability. As automotive and structural applications increasingly demand components that are both lightweight and strong, addressing this cracking problem has become essential for the practical use of these advanced materials.

## The Proposed Method

The present method addresses this cracking issue through a cold press working process that employs a free bending technique. Unlike conventional forming approaches that may constrain material movement in ways that intensify localized stresses, this method is specifically designed to manage how material behaves during deformation.

The core innovation lies in the incorporation of a material inflow facilitating portion positioned near the blank area that is destined to become the inner-side flange. This feature is strategically located to influence how the sheet material moves during the forming operation.

## How the Method Prevents Cracking

By providing this material inflow facilitating portion, the approach actively increases the flow of material from the end portion of the blank into the flange region. When the curved portion is formed, the additional material drawn in from the end portion compensates for the deformation demands placed on the inner circumferential flange. This supplemental material flow relieves the concentration of compressive stresses that would otherwise cause the material to buckle, wrinkle, or crack.

As a result, the method effectively prevents crack formation during forming, enabling the successful production of curved press components from ultra-high tensile strength steel sheets. This advancement allows manufacturers to take full advantage of the superior strength-to-weight properties of these materials while maintaining the structural integrity and dimensional quality of the finished components.

# Abstract

A method for manufacturing press-formed components from ultra-high tensile strength steel sheets that effectively prevents cracking in flange portions during the forming process. The disclosed method addresses the persistent problem of edge cracking and fracture that commonly occurs when forming steel sheets having tensile strengths of 980 MPa or greater, which exhibit reduced ductility and heightened sensitivity to strain concentration at sheet edges.

The manufacturing method comprises providing an ultra-high tensile strength steel sheet blank having a predetermined flange-forming region, and press-forming the blank in a manner that controls strain distribution along the flange edge. According to the invention, the flange region is formed while managing the sheet edge condition and localized deformation to maintain strain below a critical threshold at which cracking initiates. In certain embodiments, the method includes optimizing the blank edge geometry, controlling the punch-die clearance, and configuring the tooling to distribute forming strain away from vulnerable edge locations.

The disclosed technique enables the production of complex-shaped press components, such as automotive structural members, with high dimensional accuracy and without flange cracking, thereby permitting the use of thinner, higher-strength steel sheets to reduce component weight while maintaining structural integrity. The method achieves improved yield and productivity in the manufacture of high-strength press-formed parts.

---

*Note: This is a template abstract. For an actual patent filing, the specific technical parameters, novel features, and claims should be tailored to your particular invention and reviewed by a qualified patent attorney.*

# Summary: Press-Forming Curved Metal Components Without Flange Cracks

## The Problem Being Solved

When press-forming curved metal components (particularly those with an L-shaped or curved profile viewed from above), the flange portions are prone to **cracking**. This occurs because:

- During forming, material along the outer curve of the flange gets **stretched** (tension)
- Material along the inner curve gets **compressed** (leading to wrinkling)
- These stresses concentrate at the flange edges, causing cracks especially in high-strength steels

## Typical Invention Approach

Patents in this area generally describe methods that manage material flow to prevent these defects. Common technical features include:

**1. Multi-Stage Forming**
- Using two or more press steps rather than a single stroke
- An **intermediate/preform shape** is created first, then formed to final geometry
- The preform intentionally provides "excess material" that feeds into the flange during final forming, reducing tension

**2. Controlled Material Distribution**
- Shaping the blank so material is directed toward areas that would otherwise thin and crack
- Managing the blank's initial contour/outline to optimize material availability

**3. Specialized Tooling**
- A die, punch, and blank holder (pad) configuration
- Controlled clamping/restraint of specific regions during forming to guide metal flow

## Key Benefit

The method allows manufacturers to produce **curved, flanged components** (such as automotive structural parts—frame members, reinforcements) from **high-strength steel** while avoiding flange cracking, enabling lighter, stronger parts.

---

**Note:** This is a general summary based on typical patents in this field. If you can provide the **specific patent number, title, or the actual text**, I can give you a precise and accurate summary of that particular invention's claims and methods.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how to cold press a blank of ultra-high tensile strength steel to form a curved press component while avoiding cracks on the inner circumferential flange.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cold Pressing Ultra-High Tensile Strength Steel (UHSS) for Curved Components

Cold pressing UHSS (typically 980 MPa and above) is challenging because these materials have limited ductility and high springback. Avoiding cracks on the inner circumferential flange—where compressive circumferential stress causes wrinkling *or* tensile stress causes splitting—requires careful process control.

## Understanding the Failure Mechanism

The **inner flange** (a concave/shrink flange) experiences **circumferential compression**, while stretch flanges experience tension. Cracks on inner flanges typically arise from:

- **Localized thinning** at tight radii
- **Strain concentration** exceeding the Forming Limit Curve (FLC)
- **Edge condition defects** from blanking (micro-cracks propagate)
- **Excessive springback compensation** causing over-strain

---

## Key Process Strategies

### 1. Optimize the Blank Edge Condition
The blank's cut edge is the single biggest crack initiator.

- Use **fine blanking** or **laser cutting with controlled heat input**
- Avoid excessive burr, work-hardened, or micro-cracked edges
- Consider **edge deburring/rolling** to relieve residual stress
- Target a smooth, defect-free sheared surface (minimize the fracture zone)

### 2. Optimize Blank Geometry (Development)
- Perform **blank shape optimization** so material distribution matches the flange demand
- Add **relief notches or gussets** at the inner flange to reduce compressive crowding
- Use trimming line adjustments derived from **forming simulation** (see below)

### 3. Control Radii and Draw Geometry
- Use the **largest permissible die/punch radii** (typically ≥ 5–8× sheet thickness for UHSS)
- Avoid sharp corner transitions that concentrate strain
- Consider **multi-stage forming** rather than single-hit to distribute strain

### 4. Blank Holder Force (BHF) Management
- Apply **variable/segmented blank holder force** — lower BHF near the inner flange to allow material inflow, reducing tensile thinning
- Use **draw beads selectively** to restrain metal only where needed
- Too much restraint → splitting; too little → wrinkling

### 5. Lubrication
- Apply **high-performance dry-film or extreme-pressure lubricants** to reduce friction, improve material flow, and lower forming stress
- Ensure even coverage on flange contact zones

### 6. Tooling Design
- Manufacture tools from **high-grade tool steel** with surface coatings (e.g., CVD/PVD) to resist galling
- Include **precise clearances** (slightly larger than sheet thickness to prevent pinching)
- Consider **cushion pins / nitrogen gas springs** for controlled counter-pressure

---

## Recommended Workflow

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | **FEA simulation** (e.g., AutoForm, PAM-STAMP) using accurate UHSS material cards |
| 2 | Evaluate results against the **FLD/FLC** for necking/splitting risk |
| 3 | Optimize blank shape, radii, BHF, and draw beads iteratively |
| 4 | Compensate for **springback** in tool geometry |
| 5 | Build tools; run **tryout with strain-gauge grids** on physical blanks |
| 6 | Validate edge quality and inspect flange for micro-cracks |

---

## Additional Considerations

- **Multi-stage / progressive forming**: Break the deformation into steps to keep incremental strain below the FLC.
- **Warm forming alternative**: If cold forming repeatedly cracks, mild pre-warming (150–300 °C) can improve ductility while still being "cold-ish" relative to hot stamping. (Not true cold pressing, but a fallback.)
- **Springback compensation**: UHSS springs back significantly; over-bending and die-face compensation are essential to hit tolerance without imposing extra corrective strain later.

---

⚠️ **Note:** Because UHSS behavior is grade-specific (DP, CP, martensitic, etc.), always use the **exact material's n-value, r-value, and FLC** in your simulations. General rules of thumb can be misleading for a specific grade.

If you can share the **steel grade, sheet thickness, flange radius, and target geometry**, I can give more specific guidance on radii ratios, BHF ranges, or blank development.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical description of a free bending press method that introduces a material inflow facilitating portion to prevent flange cracking.
counterfactuals.output:
# Technical Description: Free Bending Press Method with Material Inflow Facilitating Portion

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates to a press forming method for bending sheet metal workpieces, and more particularly to a free bending (air bending) press method that incorporates a material inflow facilitating portion to prevent flange cracking during the bending operation.

## Background

In conventional free bending press operations, a workpiece is supported on the shoulders of a die and pressed by a punch without the material bottoming out against the die cavity. During bending of workpieces having pre-existing flanges, edge features, or complex peripheral geometries, tensile stresses concentrate at the flange region. When these localized tensile strains exceed the material's forming limit, cracking initiates at the flange edge, resulting in defective parts and reduced yield.

## Summary of the Invention

The disclosed method introduces a **material inflow facilitating portion** formed in or adjacent to the flange region prior to or during bending. This feature promotes controlled material flow toward the deformation zone, thereby reducing peak tensile strain at the flange edge and preventing crack formation.

## Detailed Description

### 1. Apparatus Configuration

The forming apparatus comprises:

- **Punch:** An upper tool having a working radius (R_p) configured to contact the workpiece along the intended bend line.
- **Die:** A lower tool defining a V-shaped or U-shaped opening with shoulder radii (R_d) and a die width (V) selected according to workpiece thickness (t), typically V = 6t to 12t for free bending.
- **Material Inflow Facilitating Portion:** A geometric provision—such as a recess, relief pocket, bead, or contoured clearance—positioned at the die shoulder or workpiece flange region to accommodate and guide inflowing material.

### 2. Material Inflow Facilitating Portion

The material inflow facilitating portion may be embodied in one or more of the following forms:

**(a) Pre-formed relief notch or slit:**
A shallow relief is introduced at the flange terminus prior to bending. This interrupts the continuous tensile path along the flange edge, allowing localized material to draw inward rather than stretch to failure.

**(b) Contoured die shoulder relief:**
A localized enlargement of the die opening or a tapered clearance near the flange, permitting the flange material to flow into the relief volume during punch descent.

**(c) Compensating bead or gather:**
A pre-formed convex gather (excess material reservoir) established in the blank adjacent to the flange. During bending, this stored material feeds into the tension zone, offsetting the required elongation.

### 3. Method Steps

**Step 1 — Blank Preparation:**
A sheet metal blank is provided. The material inflow facilitating portion is formed in the flange region either by an upstream operation (blanking, coining, or notching) or is defined by tooling geometry.

**Step 2 — Positioning:**
The blank is located on the die shoulders such that the intended bend line is centered over the die opening and the material inflow facilitating portion is aligned with the flange region prone to cracking.

**Step 3 — Free Bending Stroke:**
The punch descends, contacting the blank and driving it into the die opening. The workpiece bends about the punch radius while remaining supported only at the die shoulders (three-point bending), without contacting the die bottom.

**Step 4 — Controlled Material Inflow:**
As bending proceeds, tensile strain develops at the flange edge. The material inflow facilitating portion permits adjacent material to migrate into the deformation zone, redistributing strain and maintaining local strain below the forming limit.

**Step 5 — Release:**
The punch retracts. The bend angle is achieved to the target value, with springback accounted for by punch overtravel. The finished flange is free of edge cracking.

### 4. Governing Relationships

The effectiveness of strain reduction may be characterized by:

- **Local strain reduction:** ε_flange (with inflow) < ε_flange (baseline) < ε_forming-limit
- **Inflow volume balance:** The volume of the facilitating portion should approximate the volume deficit that would otherwise be supplied by flange elongation.
- **Bend angle control:** θ_final is governed by punch penetration depth (d) and die width (V), independent of die bottoming, preserving the flexibility characteristic of free bending.

## Advantages

1. **Crack prevention:** Redistribution of tensile strain eliminates flange edge cracking without altering base material grade.
2. **Process flexibility:** Retains the multi-angle capability of free bending; a single die may produce multiple bend angles.
3. **Reduced tooling force:** Lower forming loads compared to bottoming or coining methods.
4. **Cost efficiency:** Minimal additional tooling; the facilitating portion may be integrated into existing blanking operations.

## Claims (Illustrative)

1. A free bending press method comprising positioning a workpiece having a flange on the shoulders of a die, and bending said workpiece with a punch without bottoming, wherein a material inflow facilitating portion is provided at the flange region to guide material into the deformation zone and prevent flange cracking.

2. The method of claim 1, wherein the material inflow facilitating portion comprises a pre-formed relief notch at the flange terminus.

3. The method of claim 1, wherein the material inflow facilitating portion comprises a compensating gather of excess material established prior to bending.

---

*Note: This description is a general technical draft. For patent filing or production implementation, specific dimensional parameters, material specifications, and empirical validation data should be incorporated.*

# ABSTRACT

A press working method for forming high-strength steel automotive components having curved portions and flanges, which suppresses springback and dimensional inaccuracy while preventing wrinkling and cracking during forming. The method comprises forming a metal blank of high-strength steel into an intermediate shape having a curved portion extending in a longitudinal direction and a flange portion continuous with the curved portion, and subsequently press forming the intermediate shape into a final product shape. During at least one of the forming steps, a constraining force is applied to a selected region of the blank corresponding to the curved portion to control material flow, thereby reducing residual stress that causes springback along the curved portion. The flange portion is formed such that stretching or compression of material at an edge of the flange is minimized, mitigating edge cracking and wrinkling in the high-strength steel. The resulting automotive component exhibits improved dimensional accuracy along the curved portion and flange, enabling the use of high-strength steel sheets having a tensile strength of 590 MPa or greater for weight reduction of vehicle body structures such as pillars, members, and reinforcements.
